As I recall, part (b) concerning the use of funds by a provincial government for purposes other than medicare was not included in the original motion. I think this certainly is a sore point with regard to the province of Ontario, and I am glad to see that that part has been added to the motion which is before the House today. I should like to review for a moment some of the background of the Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Act, which came into effect on July 1, 1958, and the Medical Care Act, established in 1966. I think hon. members will have a better understanding of the intent and purpose of these important pieces of legislation.
The Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Act provides for federal contributions to participating provinces for a specified share of costs incurred by provinces in respect of public hospital insurance programs which they administer. The federal share of costs represents 50 per cent of sharable costs for all Canada, although the share to any individual province may be slightly more or less than the 50 per cent figure. This share is calculated on the basis of 25 per cent of average national per capita costs, multiplied by the eligible insured population in each province.
The act specifies that insured services shall include the standard in-patient services provided by hospitals, as well as out-patient treatment and diagnostic services provided. Excluded from cost sharing are t.b. hospitals and sanatoria, hospitals for the mentally ill, and institutions that provide custodial care, such as nursing homes and homes for the aged. The federal government enters into agreements with the provinces and these agreements
May 31, 1971

cannot be terminated or amended unilaterally by the federal government except by giving five years notice.
The Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Act is subject to the "interim arrangements" legislation which provides machinery for "opting out". So far, however, only the province of Quebec has exercised this authority. Recent statements by the treasurer of the province of Ontario and, to some extent, by the new premier as well, give us cause for wondering whether that province will be exercising this machinery for opting out at some time in the future. I certainly hope that will not be the case, Mr. Speaker. It seems to me that if major provinces with a large percentage of the population opt out of the federal plan, the overriding value of the program will be diminished.
The act, in its present form, permits provincial hospital insurance plans to make authorized charges directly to patients for insured services, but excluding charges by way of premium or other sum not related to a specific service, and these charges are not cost sharable by the federal government. Moreover, authorized charges are not acceptable to the federal government if they exceed 10 per cent of the cost of services. Variations, Mr. Speaker, exist in provincial hospital insurance plans because the act was designed to establish basic minimum levels of coverage; to allow provinces freedom to choose the method of raising their own share of costs; and because of the "opting out" feature of the legislation. Several provinces levy co-insurance and deterrent charges, but in all cases provision is made by these provinces for the payment of authorized charges on behalf of persons who would otherwise not be able to pay, or would be financially embarrassed by such charges. In other words, Mr. Speaker, no Canadian is denied necessary hospital care because of inability to pay.
The Medical Care Act establishes a grant-in-aid program whereby the federal government is empowered to make financial contributions to those provinces which operate acceptable medical care insurance plans that meet certain minimum criteria related to comprehensiveness of services, universality of coverage, portability of benefits and standards of administration. Federal funds became payable from the first of July, 1968, and are based on the national average per capita cost of insured services, excluding administrative costs, multiplied by the average number of insured persons in each province. With the exception of the Yukon, all provinces and territories have introduced provincial plans; and it is expected that the Yukon will have introduced an acceptable plan by the end of the current fiscal year.
The Medical Care Act, Mr. Speaker, embodies only four basic principles which must be incorporated and reflected in provincial medical care insurance plans. The reason for keeping these conditions few and simple is to avoid the necessity for entering into complicated signed agreements with each province, a feature of the Hospital Insurance Act. These principles are:
Use of Medicare Funds By Provinces
1.	Comprehensive coverage for all medically required services rendered by a physician or surgeon, and there can be no dollar limit or exclusions except on the grounds that the service is not medically required. Mr. Speaker, there must be no financial impediment or preclusion of service to an insured person that would deny him needed medical care. Provinces also have the latitude to include additional health services in their programs should they desire. And if there is a consensus among the provinces, additional health services may be added to the national program.
2.	Universal availability. Coverage must be available to all eligible residents of all participating provinces on equal terms and conditions. Moreover, in establishing a plan, coverage must be available to at least 90 per cent of the eligible population-a figure that went up to 95 per cent from April 1, 1971. This feature ensures access to coverage by all residents and prevents premium discrimination on grounds of previous medical history, non-membership in a group or other considerations. At the same time, subsidization in whole or in part for low-income groups or individuals is permitted.
3.	Portability of benefits when the beneficiary is temporarily absent from his own province or when moving from one participating province to another. Portability ensures that coverage is not lost as a consequence of moving from place to place within Canada.
4.	Non-profit administration. Public authorities administering medical care insurance plans are accountable to the provincial authority for all financial transactions.
Because the conditions have been kept simple, a province may qualify for shared federal financial support by reaching a federal-provincial understanding as to the nature of the particular provincial plan that is appropriate and acceptable for federal cost sharing. This gives each province considerable leeway to develop its own plan in the manner that best meets the particular requirements and circumstances of the province while still meeting essential national criteria. While it is true that the Medical Care Act does not preclude imposition of a utilization fee, the act clearly specifies that any such charge must not impede or preclude access to insured services by insured persons. In other words, no feature of a provincial medical care plan may deny insured services to the Canadian public.
I would add that the federal government does not especially favour utilization charges because we do not believe that such fees effectively control costs in the long run. However, provinces have the right under the Medical Care Act to determine in what manner the provincial share of medicare shall be financed and federal contributions under the act are made regardless of whether or not utilization fees are levied, providing the four essential criteria I have mentioned are met. For the information of this place, only one province has seen fit to levy utilization fees under its medical care insurance plan.
I turn now, Mr. Speaker, to the benefits to Canadians resulting from the hospital care and medical care acts which puts Canadians among the best medically cared

for people in the world. Our health coverage is universal, of a high standard, administered publicly, not by private carrier, and is portable virtually throughout Canada. These plans ensure that the less endowed provinces receive the same basic standards of coverage as the more affluent provinces and ensure that hospital and medical care is available to all Canadians. If I may refer again to the deterrent or utilization charges referred to in the hon. member's motion, as I have already stated such charges are allowable under the Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Act and I do believe that these form the raison d'etre for the motion before the House.
Concerning medicare, the federal government does not favour this method of provincial financing because we believe it can cause undue hardship to persons having only limited financial means and who as a group have greatest need to unfettered access to medical care without hindrance of any kind. Unless such charges are set at a level high enough to hinder or deter access to services, they are of little consequence. If such fees are high enough to deter, then they are self-defeating. In this regard there is no evidence to suggest that in the long run they naturally affect the level of utilization of service or the total cost of care. All they achieve is a transfer from the paying agency to the patient at the time when the patient is least able to afford such charges.
It is on the principle that a utilization fee will deter persons from running to the doctor for the most trivial matters that such fees are imposed. This reasoning is based on the false premise that only the poor make unnecessary demands on the service; the deterrent is seldom high enough to deter the more affluent user. I would quote Mr. Justice Hall, in a speech delivered in Saskatchewan in 1964, as follows:
Stripped of all sophistry and regarded in their naked application, the so-called deterrents are a tax on the poor predicated upon the fallacious assumption that it is only the poor that would ask for frivolous services.
In 1968 Saskatchewan introduced deterrent charges. Initially this resulted in a decline in utilization of medical care services. However, today utilization now exceeds the previous level of use. It is too early to determine whether this fee has deterred anyone from seeking or receiving needed medical care, but studies in this regard are being conducted. I would also like to mention the peculiar backlash that can occur when utilization fees are imposed. Once over the initial shock, many of the general public increase their use of services, feeling that as they have to pay directly for the service they might as well use it at the slightest provocation.
I should, in fairness to the Saskatchewan plan, mention that the province has agreed to pay the utilization fee on behalf of those receiving public assistance, that it pays the fee for patients receiving "statutory benefits" for cancer, tuberculosis or mental health care and that any citizen may apply for special assistance to meet the utilization fee should his circumstances require it. Additionally, doctors and hospitals are encouraged to report to provincial authorities patients not in receipt of public assistance who could be embarrassed by the fee.
On this basis, Saskatchewan has introduced a family ceiling of $180 for combined utilization fees for hospital and medical care. The fee per doctor's office call is $1.50, and for a doctor's house call or hospital emergency visit $2. The hospital insurance fees are $2.50 per day for the first 30 days, $1.50 per day for the next 60 days and no charge after 90 days. A charge of $1.50 is also made for each outpatient physiotherapy visit. Other provinces also charge hospital utilization fees which on the whole are quite nominal.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, with respect to part (a) of the hon. member's motion, the federal government's position regarding utilization fees is consonant with the hon. member's intent. The federal government certainly does not favour such fees being imposed under the Medical Care Act. However, it is our belief that experience with utilization fees will shortly lead to their abandonment because they do not achieve the purpose for which they were intended.
With respect to the Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Act, generally speaking payments by the federal government to the provinces for hospital insurance are in the form of advance payments and final payments. Monthly advance payments are based on 25 per cent of the provincial disbursements for the previous month and 231 per cent of the estimated national per capita costs applicable to the number of insured persons in the province at the end of the month. Under this arrangement, advance payments have always been much less than the provincial disbursements already made, usually approximating 50 per cent of the provincial disbursement of the previous month. Final payments under hospital insurance are made approximately two years following the actual disbursements by the province. It would therefore appear that the proposed amendment concerning the application of federal moneys by a province would not be appropriate in so far as the Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Act is concerned because the objectives of the amendment are already, quite clearly, being achieved.
With regard to part (b) of the hon. member's motion, this would, as I say, seem to be aimed at Ontario where the level of premiums set may be sufficient to carry the plan's costs from October 1, 1969, through the entire fiscal year 1970-71 without using the federal contributions at all, when one takes into account provincial funds previously being spent for insured services and which were still presumably available for this purpose. However, if the premium level were to remain unchanged, within several further years the accumulated surplus would be gradually used up. While one might disagree, as I do, with Ontario setting the initial level of its premiums as high as it did, it would seem clear that the people of Ontario are at least ensured that there will be no need to increase the premium level for some years.
I recall that when this step was taken in 1968 the share of the federal government amounted to over $170 million a year. I thought it rather unusual that at the same time the province of Ontario raised the premium level from

May 31, 1971

what was only $10 a year to $20 a year. It was a great revelation to those of us in Ontario, in view of this tremendous amount of money coming in from the federal government, that the premiums were raised. I think everyone living in the province at the time expected premiums to drop by one half, because supposedly the federal government was paying one half of the cost. As I say, instead of that the premiums were increased.
The hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre indicated in his remarks a few moments ago that there was a surplus, I believe, of $30.9 million in the fiscal year 1970-71 and that in this fiscal year under the OHSIP program there will be a surplus of $7.6 million. I would join with hon. members in commending the hon. member for his motion; there are many aspects of it with which I agree.

subtopic: MEDICARE-SUGGESTED DISQUALIFICATION OF PROVINCES IMPOSING DETERRENT FEES OR FAILING TO USE FUNDS FOR MEDICAL SERVICES ONLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker I have no hesitation in commending the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre (Mr. Benjamin) for introducing this motion. From experience I have gained in one section of this great nation of Canada, I can state there should be no deterrent fees of this sort and that everything should be done to help those in need, regardless of the cost.
I understand there may be some constitutional problems and I hope that at the next federal-provincial conference, soon to be held, the minister will use his influence to overcome some of the existing anomalies under the Medical Care Act and the Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Act in order that we have a universal plan that will provide care for all those in need.
I have some figures regarding the cost of health services which it might be worth while quoting. The cost under the health services program is $7 million, under the health insurance and resources program over $1 billion, under the medical services program $49 million, and the cost of the Medical Research Council is $36 million. I understand that deterrent fees are used in the United Kingdom to prevent over-use and abuse of the program there.
I hope that a motion will be put forward soon seeking to reintroduce under the health resources program legislation to provide funds to establish medical centres, hospitals and other services, and to induce doctors to visit our more remote and isolated communities. People living there are not worried about referral and deterrent fees, because they cannot even afford to travel vast distances in order to see a doctor. This is a ridiculous state of affairs.
Let me give the House an example of what I mean. Three days ago when visiting a community in my area I met a fisherman who over the years had built his own home with his savings. His wife had suffered a heart attack and was paralysed. He went to the welfare department to get some help in order to employ a girl or somebody to look after his wife while he was out fishing, and his application for assistance was refused. As a result, he had to build himself a shack right on the beach, bring his paralysed wife to the shack and leave her in bed while he went fishing for an hour or two. He
Use of Medicare Funds By Provinces
would then have to return ashore after a couple of hours' fishing to see how his wife was. And this sort of situation exists in a great, affluent country like Canada!
Let me give another example. I know of a child who had to wait for one year for spectacles. When he finally received them, they were no good to him because his eyesight had deteriorated even further in the interim. I also know of the case of a lady who had no legs, heart trouble and high blood pressure and was confined to bed; but because she had been cared for by her family, her social assistance payments were reduced. I suggest that situations like these should be given attention and that we must steer our efforts in this direction.
Since it is obvious that all members who have spoken are in favour of the motion, and since the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre has mentioned that the minister is in agreement with his motion, I fail to see why we should speak any further on the matter. I just want to put in my two cents' worth by saying the government of Canada must realize that we need medical care centres and more doctors and services for the needy who cannot provide for themselves, such as the blind, the incapacitated and the undernourished. More attention must be paid to such people. Without keeping the House any longer, I commend the hon. member for his motion and hope the government will agree to amend the act in order to make provision for the kind of care described by the hon. member.

The second method of equalizing health care services would be for the federal government to operate a health insurance plan limited to collecting taxes and making payments in respect of insured services. However, provincial governments have jurisdiction over the most important elements of the provision of hospital and medical services such as the operation of hospitals, provision of health personnel, organization of services, quality of care, and so forth. It can readily be seen that a federal insurance plan which had no control over matters such as I have just mentioned would be largely ineffectual in meeting the basic goals of ensuring that insured persons received high quality care at reasonable cost.
A third method of equalizing health care services for Canadians is that taken by the federal government in respect of hospital and medical care insurance programs, namely, through the medium of providing federal financial assistance under certain conditions to the provinces to help them operate their own programs. You can see that this method not only recognizes the constitutional realities but also the varying abilities of the provinces to finance necessary health services. This alternative, at the same time, effectively ensures that the provinces establish and maintain relatively uniform health insurance plans across the country. In my opinion this is the most practical approach to the problem of health care in the Canadian context.
In a country as large as Canada with highly mobile population, health and medical care must be available for Canadians should they move from province to province. To achieve portability of benefits, hospital and medical care plans must be integrated as far as possible so that the individual citizen, should he move, would retain coverage until he could obtain comparable protection in his new province of residence. Only through federal participation in hospital and medicare programs is portability made possible.
There is one further aspect of federal involvement in the health of Canadians which bears mentioning. In essence, this relates to the fact that research and technology related to the provision of health care transcend provincial boundaries. The advances being made by medical science must be available to all levels of government, and much of the responsibility for ensuring that high standards of health care are available for all Canadians falls on the shoulders of the federal government which carries out or sponsors research in the health field. Moreover, the federal government assists the provinces financially in their efforts to achieve this very desirable goal.
In respect of the patient making any direct financial contribution to the doctor on the grounds that there should be no financial impediment to anyone seeking medical advice, there has been some objection. This case
would be stronger if the doctors were bound to accept the amounts paid by the plan as payment in full. This is not the case. For example, the Ontario medical association believes 40 per cent of doctors charge their patients directly an amount equal to 10 per cent of the Ontario Medical Services Insurance Plan payment even though no so-called deterrent fees are in force. The public naturally prefers not to pay anything in the way of an extra bill, a deterrent fee or a deductible. These methods are therefore somewhat politically unacceptable, except perhaps for specified limitations.
I have not made any reference to the task force, which I thought I might have time to do this afternoon. I will refrain from doing so. In conclusion, it is my opinion that the motion before the House-presented, I am sure, with the best intentions-is, when the facts are understood, unduly restrictive and constraining to the provinces. Indeed, it is sad that the valuable time of the House should be spent debating this matter, because I feel that had the hon. member looked into his proposal more closely he would have realized the intent of his motion is covered by existing legislation.
If the hon. member is of the opinion that needed hospital or medical service is being denied Canadian citizens through the imposition of utilization fees, he should be prepared to bring these cases to the attention of the federal or provincial authorities, whichever the case may be.

subtopic: POST OFFICE ACT
subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING STAMP AGENTS' COMMISSION, LETTER MAIL PREPARATION ARRANGEMENTS, EXTRAORDINARY SERVICES, MEMBERS' MAIL, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at five o'clock while discussing Bill C-240, to amend the Post Office Act, I suggested that no arm of the
government or no department of government could be expected to do a good job when the minister was being shifted around from this department to that and when ministers were steadily coming and going from the Post Office. I do not think it is fair to the Post Office to be downgraded in this fashion or to expect any minister to do the job required in this department when there is so much shifting around. I suggest to the minister and to the government that if they are to do the necessary job in reorganizing the Post Office Department or in just running it properly, this practice should not continue and there should be some consistency to allow the minister to develop the expertise required in running the department.
The main thrust of what is proposed is a further major increase in the first-class ordinary letter rate. Three years ago local first-class letters were handled for four cents, while onward letters were handled for five cents. These rates were increased to a flat six cents. This was a 50 per cent raise in local first-class rates and a 20 per cent raise in onward rates. This was accompanied by a major reduction in service to the five-day system.
It is now proposed to again increase this rate of a flat seven cents and, further, to increase it once more to eight cents by the start of next year. This will represent a 100 per cent increase in the local mail delivery rate of ordinary letters and a 60 per cent increase in the onward letter rate in four years.
No increase in rate at this time is proposed for second-class mail.
I was interested to hear the minister say that a study on this subject is under way. I do not want to be critical and say whether these people should pay more or less at present, in view of the fact that the minister thought it worth while to make a study. Obviously he is doing something in this regard and I would be willing to leave this matter until the study is completed.
Post Office Act
With the exception of this comment, we have indicated in this House or have had indicated to us time and again that Time and Reader's Digest get by very easily here and that we might pick up $1 million or $2 million if we were to put them on a special rate. I would recommend to the minister that he take a hard look at this matter. Over the past 10 years this category of second-class mail has caused a loss to the Post Office Department of $200 million and it is forecast to lose another $30 million this year. Of the second-class mail, the loss of only $2.3 million was attributable to carrying rural weekly newspapers the circulation of which is under 10,000.
Over the years the Post Office has done quite well with first-class mail. In 1969-70 the loss on that mail was only $360,000 out of a total business of approximately half a billion dollars. In the main this mail is paying for itself. One might argue that it should continue to do so, but if this is the case why does the minister not consider that other categories of mail should not do the same? The projected loss for 1970-71 has soared to $35 million. This immense increase is due to business interruptions because of labour disputes, and salary increases beyond the 1970-71 estimates. An estimated loss of $35 million equals approximately three cents per week per Canadian.
A deficit of $33 million is forecast by the Post Office Department on third-class mail, some of it junk mail, in
1970-71. No increase in rates for this class of mail is proposed. The minister indicates that I may be mistaken. I will be happy to listen to him again. I listened fairly carefully the first time he spoke, but if I find I am in error I will be happy to apologize. When we are talking about second-class mail, at least there is a study of what should or should not be done with regard to it, but I did not hear a case put forward by the minister as to why there should not be an increase in third-class mail rates. The next time the minister speaks I should like to hear him make a case on why third-class mail should not pay its way. I would recommend that he explain to us why it should not.
I oppose a further increase in first-class mail rates. The great bulk of first-class mail is in the form of bills from or cheques to telephone, hydro, oil companies and other businesses. It is consumer mail. If the first-class mail rate is increased again, these concerns will undoubtedly pass that increase in their costs on to their customers. Hence, ordinary letter writers using first-class mail will be paying more for their stamps and will be charged more through bills for utilities and other services for which they are billed through the mail.
A further substantial raise in postal rates affecting consumers should be opposed as inflationary. The present loss on first-class mail is but three cents a week per capita. It can be argued that the basic Post Office service to Canadians using first-class mail, and to some extent second-class mail, is part of our communications media and cannot entirely be priced on a specific dollar and cent basis.
In my opinion there is a good case to be made for assistance to non-profit, health and cultural societies the

May 31, 1971
Post Office Act
success of whose efforts depends much upon their ability to communicate by mail. There is a case to be made for their receiving, if they qualify, a certain amount of federal financial aid earmarked to pay for the margin between what the non-profit societies can pay and what the Post Office should have in revenue so as to avoid being unfairly charged with carrying mail at a loss. I commend this thought to the minister and to the government. We have the examples of the Canada Council, the National Film Board and the CBC by which to judge whether, without loss to the Post Office, non-profit public or semi-public services can be assisted.
I think we must take a new, hard look at second and third-class mail. As I have indicated, I am willing to leave second-class mail rates as they are in view of the study being made. No increase has been proposed for these classifications at present. They are both, to a certain extent, services carrying profit-oriented, business or promotional mail and both these services lose the Post Office a great deal of money.
I think it is interesting to look at third-class mail and to realize that business can be profitable if mass mailing and handling can be organized. It is a fact of life of the printing business that the major cost is in the first or smaller number of pieces. If a greater volume is involved and it is handled efficiently, the unit cost of third-class mail is reduced and the revenue is increased. In my view, much of the third-class mail is not wanted by the mass of Canadians. It is mail which the business houses want to get in the letter boxes. It is mail that may be desirable for the Post Office to encourage because, properly processed and handled, it can make money for the Post Office or at least reduce the cost.
However, we find that the anticipated loss on third-class mail in 1971-72 will be no less than $38 million. Why should that be? This is, or could be, to a large degree profit-oriented mail. Why should the third-class rate not be increased to the point where it will at least more nearly pay for carriage of this mail? We should press for renegotiation of the international postal agreement which has involved losses for Canada in carrying U.S. mail, much of it printed. The international agreement does not take into consideration that Canada and the United States exchange, free of charge, mail handling services while one country has a population ten times that of the other.
I also urge an examination through a commission or special inquiry of the various subsidies and charges borne by the postal service in order to bring out the facts of costing and to provide a clear picture showing who pays for what. The purpose of this would be to rectify the outmoded system still in vogue whereby the Post Office provides free services to some departments while other departments provide the Post Office with very valuable services such as free accommodation in buildings.
If the minister is not satisfied with what I have said relating to some of these items, I would be happy to have him tell us that the Post Office does operate under a proper cost accounting system: I should like him to prove

to the House that this is the way in which the Post Office is run. Myself and many other Canadians, I am sure, are not absolutely certain that this is the way it is done. If we are in error, we would be happy to hear from the minister.
We want to know the findings of the body which studied the value of turning the Post Office into a Crown corporation rather than continuing it as a department of the government headed by a minister. This question has been much debated. If the government decides to turn the department into a Crown corporation, we want advance information on such studies before deciding whether or not we agree.
We urge modernization of equipment, procedures and administration beyond what has been achieved so far. In this regard the Post Office is in the same position as the telephone companies were a few years ago before they made their operations as automatic as possible. It is possible to end the physical distribution of old age pension and family allowance cheques, totalling scores of millions of letters a month, by using an electronic mail service, with the value of the cheques being deposited in the banks by electronic impulse. While pressing for efficiency we must seek to preserve and extend the gains made by postal workers since they attained collective bargaining. Phase-outs of jobs in certain postal categories must not be made at the expense of the employees. For instance, while the new sortating procedure is estimated to improve efficiency and reduce per unit handling costs by means of greater speed, it should not result in lay-offs of employees over the next several years.
What I am saying is that, hopefully, any modernization of equipment within the Post Office will be achieved on a basis that will cause the least possible damage to the employees involved. When we consider that there may be
50,000	people working for the Post Office, we can see that this department affects a great many people. We oppose the increase in first class mail rates and for this reason we will support the amendment of the official opposition.

Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity Bill C-240 presents to discuss not only the amendments to the Post Office Act but also matters in regard to the general operations of the Post Office. I am very happy to see the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Laing) in the chamber tonight, because for two years he and I have been trying to arrange a mutual visit to the beautiful little village of Elora where two years ago he was kind enough to stop the building of a new post office. In that connection I hope the Postmaster General will talk to his officials and ask them to take another look at the building and at the accommodation required, because we had a local architect look at it, a man who has designed many good buildings in Toronto, who felt that with some modifications and changes it could be retained in accordance with the wishes of the people.
May 31, 1971

Elora is a beautiful little village situated on the banks of the Grand River. A great many of the homes are built of stone. Some of the churches are built of stone. It is in the centre of the area through which the Elora road went up from Guelph. In those days it was, shall we say, a watering place. It has that background of stability which you find only in the smaller villages of Ontario. If the Minister of Public Works cannot make the trip that he has promised to make to the village, I sincerely hope the Postmaster General will have his officials meet with the officials of Public Works and agree on modifications to make this building more useful to the people who work there.
I am not one who always looks for change. I see some of the new post offices that have been built in communities, replacing old ones cast aside a few year ago- beautiful, red brick post offices which were subsequently bought by the local communities and used as municipal buildings. Those old offices could still be functional as post offices. In light of that experience, I think the officials of both departments should take a second look before deciding to demolish old post offices and erect new ones. Mr. Speaker, you and I know that many of the older buildings will still be standing when some of the new buildings being put up today will have outlived their usefulness. The present post office in Elora could be modernized without destroying its architecture.
Now I wish to say a word about this bill and in support of the amendment moved by my colleague objecting to postal rate increases. This is the second time within a very few years that we have been faced with a postal increase; and it is the same old story, that the administration needs more money for labour and renovations. In his remarks the Minister without Portfolio (Mr. Cote) indicated that within the past year they have been able to reduce the postal deficit. I believe that implementing some of the programs he has initiated and introducing more efficient means of handling and distributing mail will result in the deficit being brought down a great deal more.
When I first became a member of this House, Mr. Speaker, the Post Office used to have a surplus. That was quite a few years ago. I remember criticism being made of the then Postmaster General because the postal service was so poor. People today are still complaining about the postal service. In light of a question I asked the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Pepin) last week with respect to the census, we can only wonder about the efficiency of the postal service. As recorded at page 6075 of Hansard, I asked the minister:
In connection with the census which begins on June 1 can he explain to the House and to the people of Canada why all Canadians will not be allowed to send their returns directly to the department as will be done in cities?
In reply the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce said:
Mr. Speaker, I have a note from DBS which says that either the mail-back or pick-up system by census representatives assures confidentiality, but the pick-up system is employed in localities where, for instance, the mail service is insufficient-
Post Office Act
My riding is made up of small rural and urban communities. I think I get as good postal service as do people in the cities of Ottawa and Toronto and I can see no reason why the people of my area should be treated differently, with respect to the census, from people in Ottawa and Toronto. As was indicated by my colleague from Wellington (Mr. Hales) today, the census-taker may be your next door neighbour. He is supposed to discuss your census problems with you. In such a case there is not complete confidentiality. I plead with the Postmaster General to plead with his colleague the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce, to have an advertisement appear in all newspapers across Canada telling people in small communities that if they want to put their returns into envelopes and send them by mail to the DBS, they are free to do so. That could still be done even though tomorrow is census day.
I see no reason why people in small communities should be treated differently from city dwellers. They should be allowed to return the census form to the Dominion Bureau of Statistics by mail. There is a lot of criticism across the country on this matter, so I hope the Postmaster General will get in touch with the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce and work something out.
Referring to the amendment proposed by my colleague, it is interesting to note that the Postmaster General has indicated that 80 per cent of postal revenue is derived from business and industry. The last time postal rates were increased I remarked that it would have an inflationary effect, and now the government is doing it again. We all know that in the end the consumer pays. Although the rate for first-class mail may only be increased by two or three cents, business takes that increase into account in its profit and so we have another inflationary trend.
I wonder if the Postmaster General discussed this bill with the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Basford) before it was brought in. Does it mean that we will have another round of inflation and another round of deliberate unemployment to stop it? The increase in the third-class mail rate applies mostly to throwaway mail and catalogues of the type issued by large department stores. It is a vicious circle; the catalogues are used to promote business, but in the end it is the customer who pays for the increased cost of doing business and this, of course, includes the postage on the catalogues. I object to the proposed increase in postal rates because we have had enough inflation and enough of the unemployment that was created in an effort to curb it. I do not think that the people will stand for this again.
A previous speaker mentioned the low morale of Post Office employees. Maybe the Postmaster General has improved the morale a little, but he has a long way to go. As morale improves, efficiency will improve. He should work toward this end. This government has brought in many phasing-out programs, starting with the small post offices. In many villages the store with the post office was

May 31, 1971
Post Office Act
the hub of the community. In many cases the closing of the post office has meant that business has ceased to be profitable and merchants have had to sell out and move to the cities to try and find other employment.
The government also talks about phasing out the textile industry, and it is phasing out the farmer. Pretty soon they will be dictating how everybody in Canada may earn a living. These programs are neither fair nor just-people are being injured and ways of life are being destroyed by them. We sincerely hope that before this bill is passed the Postmaster General and the government will reconsider it. It might even be withdrawn or held back. As I have pointed out, there should be some means of controlling the deficit other than by increasing postal rates.
Another point that bothers me is that residents of small communities must pay rent for a post office box. There is door to door delivery in some rural areas and in the larger towns, but in small communities it costs $5 or $10 to have the mail put in the box. Even then it is sometimes impossible to get into the post office after hours for one's mail. I am also a little disturbed by the delegation of authority. Clause 1, subsection (3) reads:
Section 5 of the said act is further amended by adding thereto the following subsections-
There is provision for delegation of powers to assistant deputy postmasters general, regional general managers and directors of the Post Office Department. When the minister speaks in this debate I should like him to explain why these powers are delegated to non-elected officials of the Post Office Department. "Governor in Council" appears in a lot of other legislation, so I should like to know what powers are being delegated to these officials throughout the country.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, I should like to say again that I do not think these postal rate increases are necessary, because they will be inflationary and we have had enough of that.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, members who come from British Columbia are not anxious to move further east; we prefer to remain in our own province.
I should like to speak briefly on this bill and to endorse the amendment moved by the official opposition to give the legislation a six months' hoist. I believe a number of valid reasons for this have been given by various speakers and it is not my intention to repeat them this evening. Just two years ago we had a very lengthy debate on Post Office problems. That was when rates of all description were increased rather sharply. A great deal of damage was done to a number of publications in Canada. As yet, hon. members of this House have not been given a full or extensive report of what actually happened in
that connection. This should be given to us prior to our again increasing sharply postal rates on first-class mail.
Although several points have been stressed by other speakers I will refer to one or two of them again. I might say that the Public Accounts Committee discussed matters along these fines. I raised these points with officials of the department. They said they were looking into one or two matters which I will again bring to the minister's attention. I hope that the points raised will be taken care of in legislation. One of these points may sound like a small matter for people living in cities but it means a great deal for people who come from rural areas. In a city, so long as there are 2,000 postal drops there is free mail delivery. The postman comes to your home and delivers the mail through a slot in the door; it is delivered to you in your house.
In smaller communities with less than 2,000 postal drops-I happen to five in one and would not move to a city just to get the additional mail carrier service-people are charged rent for a post office box. There the postman puts the mail in the box and you must go down, collect the mail from the box and take it home.
I have raised this point before and I raise it again. This is rank discrimination against Canadians who live in rural areas. There is no escaping this fact. People of our smaller communities must take the time and incur the cost, quite frequently, involved in driving several miles or they must walk a considerable distance to the post office. Once there they are given the privilege of renting a post office box unless, of course, they desire general delivery.
I suggest to the minister that the rental charged for post office boxes be done away with. The least the minister can do is give residents of these small areas the right to obtain their mail free of charge from a post office box. In the cities, as I say, the postman comes to your door and drops the mail right at your home. Surely the least we can do is provide a box for the rural homeowner so that he may go and pick up his mail whenever it suits him. The rural dweller incurs the additional cost of having to go the the post office under his own steam, by car or by any other means he may choose. The cost varies with the distance he must travel.
I have received a number of letters on the subject and I am sure that the minister and the department have also received letters. I received a letter the other day from an individual in Fruitvale which is in my riding of Kootenay West. The writer points out that he must pay $15 a year for a certain class of post office box. If he lived in a larger centre the mail would be delivered to his home free of charge. I do not think anyone can demonstrate to me the logic in loading an additional charge upon those who live in rural areas. I have protested against this charge before and I do it again now.

speechtext:
If any group of residents in Canada deserve to be subsidized with regard to mail service or

May 31, 1971

any other service, it is our citizens who live in rural areas and who quite often are without many of the amenities of life. These amenities are concentrated in the big cities. It seems that the services of almost any department of government are more expensive in rural areas. Rural dwellers are stuck with these additional costs. In this instance we are talking about the Post Office. I again suggest to the minister that this is one of the topics which ought to be put on the agenda for discussion. He ought to talk it over with the staff of the Post Office. People in rural areas ought to be shown this consideration. I have no hesitation in making this suggestion although I know that if it is implemented the department will lose revenue. That is beside the point, however.
A good argument for subsidizing-if you want to call it that-rural post office boxes stems from the fact that two years ago when we were dealing with Post Office costs we found that Reader's Digest, an American magazine, was subsidized for delivery in Canada to the extent of $800,000, and that Time magazine was subsidized to the extent of $721,000. I do not think that situation has changed. These two magazines are being subsidized to the extent of $1,521,000. The money comes out of the pockets of taxpayers, including those who live in the rural areas. I say it would be far better to use the $1,521,000 to help those in rural areas obtain better mail service than to subsidize these two magazines.

speechtext:
Yes. At least, they have been on occasion. They have supported this government. But that is beside the point.
Let us look at the rates that will come into effect under this new piece of legislation. We find that first-class rates will be primarily affected. They will be affected seriously. The effect on individuals will be serious. The increase will constitute a truly inflationary cost with respect to the mailing of letters. On July 1, 1971, just over one month from now, first-class mail rates will increase to 7 cents a letter. Six months later, just after Christmas, this Liberal government will tell the Canadian people that, for a New Year's gift, they will be charged 8 cents for every first-class letter mailed. I say that this rate is excessively high.
Let us examine the first-class mail rates which the minister is trying to initiate with this new legislation. The 8-cent rate which will be implemented at the end of the year will cover only those letters weighing one ounce or less. For letters weighing more than 1 ounce- and many letters weigh slightly more, tipping the scale at l\ ounces-the mailing rate is to be 14 cents per letter. As you go up the scale you find that the rates increase fantastically. Perhaps I should put them on the record because some hon. members may not have examined them.
I will take the rates which will apply on January 1, 1972. These are to be the rates: 8 cents for any letter weighing 1 ounce or less; 14 cents for a letter weighing more than 1 ounce but not more than 2 ounces; 20 cents for a letter weighing more than 2 ounces but not more
Post Office Act
than 4 ounces; 32 cents for a letter weighing more than 4 ounces but not more than 8 ounces; 44 cents for a letter weighing more than 8 ounces but not more than 12 ounces, and 54 cents for a letter weighing more than 12 ounces but less than 16 ounces.
If this is not an inflationary method of increasing costs to the Canadian public, I don't know what is. I suggest to the minister that he look very closely into this question of postal rates. He should find out how these rates have affected the small weeklies and periodicals which used to circulate in abundance two or three years ago. Hundreds of them from one end of Canada to the other have been forced out of business because they could not afford the excessive increase in mailing costs. Some may say the Post Office must pay its way. But many of these little publications were part of the Canadian way of life. Many of them had their own peculiar outlook, if I might put it that way, and brought a different perspective to events which took place in various sections of Canadian activity. I believe we have lost culturally and in other ways through these papers being forced out of circulation.
We should think in terms of providing subsidies. Hon. members may ask why papers of this kind should be subsidized. But if we are to get into a discussion on subsidies, one might well ask: Why subsidize anything? A story which appeared in the Toronto Daily Star a couple of weeks ago indicated we were subsidizing the mining industry to the tune of more than $300 million. In the northern regions of Canada most of the mining firms receiving these subsidies are foreign-owned and controlled; they ship Canadian products out of the country after we have plowed a subsidy into the operation.
I say that a type of subsidy which gives something to the people of Canada is far better than giving something to a foreign corporation which exports raw resources from the country for fabrication elsewhere. The point might be debatable and the minister might wish to debate it, but I am using it by way of illustration. If he is looking to save dollars he should not be trying to whittle a little more from the average Canadian citizen who will be forced to pay excessive postal rates in many instances. The minister should be looking elsewhere for his savings.
I may be wrong, but I understand there is to be a postal convention in July at which rates are to be reviewed. I hope this is so. I made a note to the effect three or four weeks ago when we were discussing the Post Office estimates in the Public Accounts Committee. If there is to be a postal convention I suggest it is a good reason for holding over this legislation. There are a number of points which the minister should raise at the convention. If they are raised and if changes are made, he might be able to tell us that certain modifications can be made in connection with this legislation.
Here are a few facts I gleaned during one of the committee's meetings. In 1969-70 the Post Office lost $27.9 million. Of this, $3.9 million represented the loss on the mailing of daily papers. Another $2.3 million was lost on mailing weekly papers. Some of these papers, as hon.

May 31, 1971
Post Office Act
members know, can be mailed free of charge within a 40-mile radius of their place of publication. In connection with the mailing of magazines and periodicals, there was a deficit of $13.6 million of which the delivery of foreign publications mailed in Canada accounted for a loss of $2.7 million. A loss of $5.4 million was incurred in dealing with incoming United States mail.
One of the oddities of the postal structure is that although the delivery of foreign publications mailed in this country costs $2.7 million, it would have cost $5 million if it had been mailed in the United States. This does not make sense. In the circumstances, it is a good thing for Canadian taxpayers that these publications were mailed in Canada or the Post Office would have lost double the amount it did. It seems to me the whole mailing cost structure needs revision. These things should not happen. It is for this reason I say the legislation should be held over until the convention has been held and we know exactly what rates will be charged for handling mail by other nations and ourselves.
The provision of Post Office facilities is not dealt with in the bill before us but it will certainly be affected by the new regulations which are laid down. We have been promised that certain new postal facilities for Castlegar will be ready by March of next year. I believe the department should press forward with this work as quickly as possible. A new postal walk system will be started in the area, the point having been reached at which there are more than 2,000 postal drops. Let the department complete this new facility and get the new postal walk system started. I believe a number of small communities just outside the area of Castlegar, Kinnaird and Robson should also be included in this service. This would do a good deal to improve the mail service in the area, and the people there certainly need it.
While I am dealing with local matters I wish to draw to the minister's attention the fact that delivery of second and third-class mail is extremely lax in my constituency. Daily papers are sent to me and I am lucky if I get them ten days after they have been posted in Nelson. It is not unusual for me to get them two weeks or 16 days later. This is not good enough. We were told at the time rates were last revised that the mail service would improve. It has not improved; it has deteriorated. I was receiving second and third-class mail much faster than I do now. There must be some kind of tie-up somewhere that the department should investigate.
We have complained about this sort of thing, but service does not seem to improve. There is a hold-up somewhere along the line after second-class mail gets to the post office. Whether it is because the mail is slow leaving the post office of origin, or the transit of the mail is slow, I do not know; but it should not take from ten days to two weeks to send a weekly or daily paper from Nelson to Ottawa. A donkey could walk across Canada faster than that. There is no reason in this day and age to put up with a mail delivery service of this nature.
In closing, I urge the minister to hold over this legislation at least until the fall. By then we will have had a
better chance of looking into many of the points that have been raised and, I hope, will be able to make some meaningful amendments to the legislation.

subtopic: POST OFFICE ACT
subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING STAMP AGENTS' COMMISSION, LETTER MAIL PREPARATION ARRANGEMENTS, EXTRAORDINARY SERVICES, MEMBERS' MAIL, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think previous speakers have outlined many of the problems of the present day postal service but I have a few impressions that I should like to put on the record this evening. Several clauses of the bill are laudable, particularly the one that provides for the free delivery of mail to the blind. This is a very good step to have included within the postal regulations. Further, some economies may be possible as a result of the provisions of proposed new paragraphs (u) and (v) of sub-section 1 of section 5 of the act under which postal customers who prepare their mail in a manner that creates less work for postal employees will pay reduced rates. One cannot argue with the merits of these two provisions of the bill.
There are, however, very few members of this House who would agree with the increase in postal rates at this time. Some time ago I read a comparison of the cost of mailing letters and making telephone calls. Although the comparison was of the situation in the U.S.A., I think a parallel can be drawn in Canada. When telephones were first introduced into the United States you could mail something over 13,000 letters for the cost of one telephone call across the continent. Although I forget the exact figures, today you can only mail several hundred letters for the cost of one telephone call, giving a ratio of something like 20 to one. I suppose we have seen some improvements made in the field of transportation since that time, but it does make one wonder where one is going in view of the way costs between these two methods of communication have increased inversely.
Government has become involved in many ways both in the private and the public sector and a great many people disagree with this. If one were to conduct a survey across the country on whether to put departments of government on a pay-as-you-go basis, there would probably be more support for subsidizing the Post Office and postal services than any other aspect of the economy that is subject to government interference, or perhaps I should say government intervention.
There are many areas in which we are conscious of maintaining Canadian content and culture and of keeping Canadians aware that they are Canadians. As the previous speaker pointed out, some periodicals in Canada have been very useful in promoting culture, both locally and nationally. Many of these periodicals have had to go out of business, having become part of our daily life. Some of them, as it were, were institutions in themselves. By making postal rates prohibitive and causing these publications to be discontinued, we are that much poorer. We pour money into the CBC in an effort to portray the Canadian scene. Perhaps we would do better to withdraw funds from such organizations and use them to subsidize postal rates.
Comparisons have been drawn between rural and urban postal services and some of the glaring inequities have been referred to. Many communities have had to suffer a cessation of postal services. True, the population

May 31, 1971

of these communities was not great but in several cases in my own constituency the alternative means of mail delivery, while not nearly as effective in the community, often cost more than the original postal service. In many instances post offices were housed in old buildings, and while they may have been substandard they did provide a living to members of the community and gave better service than alternative mail services.
I do not think there is one member of this House who has not received letters from his constituents about the cost of post office boxes compared with general delivery costs. This has been another glaring anomaly. People pay for these boxes at additional cost, yet they do not have the service received by those on rural delivery or obtain better service than those on general delivery. The present rate structure pertaining to post office boxes can only discourage people from renting them, thus putting a greater load on the general delivery service.
Obviously, pride of workmanship in the Post Office is disappearing. There used to be a slogan that the mail must go through, though this has not been evident in recent years. I remember that five or six years ago it took about two days, and sometimes less, to get a letter from my own riding to Ottawa. Today it takes a week. Sometimes it takes only four or five days, but often two weeks. One can sense a loss of pride of workmanship in postal services in the last few years.
We all used to subscribe to a daily newspaper in my home town. I still have such a subscription. That paper was delivered by the postal service to my box one day after publication. This I can understand. There must be certain economies in the postal service and in a small rural community it may not be possible or practical to have same-day delivery. The situation today is that the paper comes in by bus, it is picked up by a delivery boy the same evening and at a cost of $5 per year less than the cost of mail delivery it is delivered the same day. I am not exaggerating the situation. If this situation exists in my community it must exist in a great many others across the country.
The rates envisaged in this bill will phase out the use of the Post Office Department. It is time we looked at this system with a view to overhauling it. There has been a gradual deterioration of mail services. There is only a fraction of the number of letters written in Canada today as were written years ago. This is a deplorable situation. If we intend to subsidize other means of transportation to promote culture and communication in Canada, the postal service should be at the top of the priority list.
The minister must be aware of a brief submitted by War Amputations of Canada. There is nothing in this bill which will have an effect on third-class mail, but many organizations such as the one to which I have referred are doing their best to be self-sufficient in carrying out an effective role in Canada. They have had difficulty because of increased postal rates. If we do not look after these organizations in some way in relation to lower postal rates, the government will be faced ultimately
Post Office Act
with an additional expense to offset their costs. Surely a lower rate is the best way to take care of this situation.
I shall not take any more time to deal with postal rates. Other members have made their points very capably. Surely, as a result of the briefs presented to the minister he is well aware of the situation. The time for talking has passed. The minister should approach the postal service situation with a view to working out a viable service in Canada of which we can all be proud.

subtopic: POST OFFICE ACT
subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING STAMP AGENTS' COMMISSION, LETTER MAIL PREPARATION ARRANGEMENTS, EXTRAORDINARY SERVICES, MEMBERS' MAIL, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a few comments before this bill to amend
the Post Office Act is referred to the committee for further study. I know the minister does not officially occupy the position of Postmaster General until his ascension under the government reorganization bill, but I should like to congratulate him as the Postmaster General. I know he is very sincere in his efforts to do a good job in this position. He is faced with great responsibility in getting the Post Office service back on the rails. Had he been Postmaster General for some time perhaps this department would not find itself in the position it is today.
This bill contains several worthy amendments. Clause 3, on page 2, suggests that the Postmaster General may delegate all or any of the powers he holds. This will add greatly to the operations of the Post Office. I have in mind one incident discussed by members of the Public Accounts Committee not long ago. One postmaster in Canada accepted bulk mail at the wrong rate; it was later found that a higher rate should have been charged. The ensuing dispute ended up in the Department of Justice which ruled that the local postmaster did not have the authority to set the postage rate which should be charged on this particular type of mail. As I understand this bill, that situation will be covered.
Hon. members of this House appreciate the clause in the bill which allows Members of Parliament free postage on four bulk mail deliveries per session. There is also a clause which provides that those operating sub post offices on behalf of the department will receive 5 per cent of their sales rather than 2 per cent. I am sure the people affected will be grateful to the minister for this change. Blind people will appreciate the changes made in the bill in respect of their mail in Canada.
The rest of the bill is comprised of increases in rates with a few other consequential changes. I am at a loss to understand why the Postmaster General has brought in increased rates for two different dates, July 1, of this year and January 1, of 1972. Perhaps he thought the changes would be easier to swallow if they were made in two separate doses. I am sure the people of Canada would much prefer to have one increase.
There is nothing in this bill which will increase the efficiency of the operations of the Post Office. This seems to be where the trouble lies. Let us consider how long it takes for a letter mailed in Ottawa to be delivered in Montreal. Two weeks ago a letter was posted on Friday night instructing the recipient to phone when the letter

May 31, 1971
Post Office Act
was received. The return phone call was not made to Ottawa until Wednesday, because it took from Friday morning to Wednesday morning tor the person to receive the letter containing the phone call instructions. Over such a short distance as from Ottawa to Montreal a person could have taken the message a lot faster on a bicycle. I cannot see anything in these amendments which will clear up such a situation.
Also, I do not see anything in the amendments to correct the situation in respect of householder mail delivery. I had a recent experience in this regard. I have bulk mail deliveries for which I pay on a per pound basis. As an example, this mail left Ottawa on May 20 and was not delivered until May 28. Another batch of mail was mailed from here, received at the local post office on Tuesday and carried by the rural mail carrier in his car from Tuesday to Saturday morning without being delivered. This type of thing must be corrected in the Post Office operation.
The Canadian office of the Shorthorn Breeders Association is located in my area. This association publishes a monthly magazine. It is taken to the post office a few days after the first of the month. The delivery of this magazine is taking as long as three weeks. The delivery service in respect of this magazine is so poor that the advertisers have threatened to withdraw their advertising unless better mail service is provided. I do not see anything in these amendments to take care of next-day delivery. I know there has been an attempt in major centres to have various boxes labelled so that if you post mail in those boxes before a certain time, next-day delivery will be guaranteed. I hope this situation will be taken care of by the regulations the department will be instituting. Previously we had next-day delivery practically anywhere in Canada, but it is now a very rare occasion on which there is next-day delivery no matter where one lives. There is nothing in these amendments to take care of such a situation.
There is a situation which was brought to the attention of the Public Accounts Committee. This is a reflection on the personnel involved, those on whom the minister depends for administration. In 1964 the Post Office Department published Christmas stamps. This was the first time it had been done. The bottom of the stamp contained the inscription "1964". The number of stamps that would be sold was overestimated to the extent that when Christmas 1964 was over, $16,000 worth of printed stamps were on hand. Nobody wanted to use 1964 stamps on their 1965 Christmas cards; therefore the department decided the only thing to do was to scrap the whole lot. The Post Office Department scrapped $16,000 worth of printed stamps because of an error on the part of those responsible for the purchase of stamps.
That surely should have been lesson enough for the Post Office Department. But no. In 1970 they again overestimated the purchase of Christmas stamps. If they had merely printed a Christmas stamp without the year on it, it could have been carried over to the next year. But, no;
they did it again. In 1970 they had about $8,000 worth of Christmas stamps left. You can go into almost any post office, ask for a 1970 Christmas stamp and obtain it. I received an Easter card saying "Happy Easter" and the envelope bore a Christmas stamp. These stamps are still being sold. This sort of thing is going on in the Post Office and it is the responsibility of the people working in that department. Unless the Postmaster General, through his deputy, sees that the people who have responsibility execute that responsibility the Post Office and its service will never improve and become efficient.
We have only to think of the sale of trucks during the strike of the Lapalme drivers in Montreal. The Post Office Department decided it should get into the business of delivering mail and therefore purchased the trucks from, I believe, Rod Service. They took an inventory of so many trucks. However, the people in the Post Office Department, in adding up the number made a mistake involving $16,000. If we are to have this type of operation by personnel in the Post Office Department we will never have an efficient service; the people of Canada will never have the service to which they are entitled.
I do not see anything in the bill to improve our stamps. I believe Canada has the worst postage stamps of any country in the world. They have no lustre, no colour, brightness or attractiveness. All one need do is receive a stamp from a country such as Jamaica and Antigua to know that our stamps are not as attractive. The Postmaster General shakes his head; he does not believe this statement. If he were to write a letter to the stamp collectors' organizations across this country and ask their honest opinion concerning Canadian stamps, I believe what I have said would be borne out to be fact.
There is no mention in these amendments of a very important point. I do not know how the minister will reconcile charging the people of Canada an increased postage rate when he is not giving them good service. I am not holding this Postmaster General responsible; he was not the Postmaster General when the situation arose. What happened in respect of the last increase is that the people of Canada were charged a higher postage rate and received less service. This is what is likely to happen again.
I believe the minister would have been smarter had he given the people real service and efficiency so that he would have just reason for asking for increased rates. The Postmaster General has no right to increase postage rate until he gives the people of Canada better service and more efficiency in the operation. The only way in which I believe he will be able to do this is to return to the six-day delivery service. Canada is the only country in the world which has tried a five-day delivery service. It has been tried long enough for us to know it will not provide service to the people of Canada.
The example I spoke of concerning a letter taking from Friday to Wednesday, over a holiday weekend, to go from here to Montreal was partly a result of the five-day delivery system. There was no delivery on Saturday and

May 31, 1971

no delivery on Monday because it was a holiday weekend. When this happens the mail piles up, cannot be handled on Tuesday and does not go out until Wednesday. Until we return to a six-day delivery system we will have this situation. I do not see how in these circumstances the people of Canada can ever be given the service this increase in price demands.
The counter service in the post office was withdrawn for many months. If you went to a post office on Saturday you found a couple of men who handed out parcels or general delivery mail, but if you wanted to buy a money order or stamps they would say, "I am sorry, but we are closed today". This is quite asinine. It might be compared to going to a department store and approaching a jewellery counter which is closed, or going to the men's department and finding it closed although the whole store is open. If you are going to run a post office, for goodness sake run a post office; don't run a half show and have the counter half open or half closed. I am glad to note that since this minister took over he has restored the counter service on Saturday mornings. I think that the next step should be to open it all day on Saturdays as it used to be, so that the people of Canada can have the service which they deserve.
The minister has a public relations job on his hands. It seems that he must get a well organized team which will work together, pull together and adopt the theory that the mail must go through. He must not try to think up excuses why it did not go through. Unless he obtains that co-operation within his organization, he will not succeed.
I must congratulate his predecessor on going out into the business field and hiring men from industry. He picked up some top-notch men who were outstanding in the business community and he transplanted them into the Post Office Department. They are now in positions of authority in the Department and I am looking for great results from this type of reorganizaton in the Post Office. I am sure that under this minister's direction we will get it. I think this minister will treat men as human beings and not as machines, as was the case before. Having made some of these changes, I have every hope that the minister will get the Post Office back on the rails so that the people of Canada will be able to say that we have as good a postal service if not better than anywhere in the world.
Now I would like to say a few words about rural post offices, some of which are in a deplorable condition. This is not really the fault of rural postmasters. The problem is that they have not been paid well enough to keep a decent place, to paint it and to make of it a respectable post office. After all, these places represent Her Majesty's mail service and they should be show places. They should be tidy, neat and a credit to Canada. I should like to say that in my community our post office is one of the show places on the main street. It is always clean and there is always a flag flying from its rooftop. It is a well operated post office. I hope we will find similar ones all across Canada.
Post Office Act
May I say in conclusion that there are many problems facing this minister and I know he will do his best to correct them. I am sure he knows that if he does not increase the efficiency of the delivery service to which the Canadian people are entitled, he will have no right to increase the rates as outlined in the amendments to the Post Office Act.
