speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is like old times to be discussing the Post Office Department, but I can hardly tell you how much I miss the hon. member for Duvernay (Mr. Kierans) in these discussions. However, I have a feeling that perhaps the Post Office will remember him even longer than I will, because he who was so excellent in many other activities and has such a great contribution to make to the understanding of the economic problems of this country could not have been more unfortunately miscast than by being placed in charge of the Post Office Department. I never quite knew whether the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) did this deliberately.
However, I am hopeful for better things from the present minister but not as hopeful as I was a few months ago, because I think he has not shown too much energy in throwing off the regrettable habits, attitudes and postures of his predecessor, these things which brought about such a decay in the service and such a multiplication in the deficits. Neither of these situations is something which a conscientious Canadian parliamentarian or postal patron would welcome.
I seem to remember that in another Parliament this same minister had a little trouble in getting through an extra soaking of the Canadian public for postal rates. Perhaps history will repeat itself.
I am sorry that this minister, for whom I personally have great affection, should be presenting a major piece of legislation the chief ingredient of which is yet another increase in the cost of postage to the people of Canada. As my colleagues have said, if this by any stretch of a partial imagination could be correlated with improved service, there might be some justification for looking upon the proposed increase with dispassion. But this is not the case. No one would talk with much enthusiasm or conviction about an improved postal service. The problem is the result of a series of costly fiascos in the administration of the Post Office Department, fiascos which have diminished the respect of the Canadian people for this important department of government and curtailed the use by the people of Canada of the Post Office Department, thereby diminishing the revenues which should flow from the public use of the department.
It is well known-and I quite agree with my colleague who has just resumed his seat-that the most egregious error under the previous Postmaster General was the cessation of service on Saturdays. He was warned that in a country of such vast distances as Canada this could not possibly be anything but a stupid and retrograde step. The events have proven the wisdom of this sad prognosis. Much of the problem of the delayed mail delivery comes from the fact that there is a blackout between Friday

May 31, 1971
Post Office Act
and Monday and that a good deal of the mail which is brought in on Friday does not move until Tuesday.
Another result is that patrons of the Post Office Department in the parcel post field are using alternative means, and daily we hear on radio the advertisements of the bus PX service. It is apparently cheaper and more efficient to use other means of transporting parcels than Her Majesty's mail. So as costly fiasco follows costly fiasco, as there is a diminution of the usage of the postal department by the people of Canada, the natural result is that those who still use it-and there are many millions who must-will have to pay more. So up goes the price of stamps yet again.
The white paper-it is a mistake to say "the" white paper-one of the plethora of white papers has forecast stamps that would cost 26 cents. We are moving toward that, Mr. Speaker, with a very unpleasant and unwelcome speed. Time was when we had five-cent stamps and six-day delivery. Then the shift was to five-day delivery and a six-cent stamp. But that is not good enough. We have to raise the ante; we have to increase the cost of stamps. No one can point out that this is in any way likely to be connected with increased service because alas, Mr. Speaker, we find that under the present jurisdiction the same old problems of employee unrest seem to plague the Canadian postal service.
Only today we hear of very serious protests from union spokesmen in the Post Office here in Ottawa; charges of far too numerous employment of casuals and charges of something even more serious, that there is a degree of nepotism involved. All of this, of course, is very disturbing to the morale of the Post Office and it seems to be a repetition of the old, old story that things are not going well in this department which was established at the time of confederation, one of the old established departments of government which, if experience should mean anything, would be expected to be a very efficient one.
I agree with those who point to this particular bill and find it inadequate in dealing with the important issues. A few months ago we were told that the guttering prospect of the estabhshment of a Crown corporation was not far away and that this was the answer. How many hundreds of thousands of dollars were spent on how many costly, elaborate and lengthy studies into the efficacy and efficiency of a Crown corporation? Now it seems that the idea, like the studies from which it was produced, is gathering dust and no one mentions the Crown corporation any more.
It seems that the only innovation we can get out of those in charge of the Post Office is something new like a new price of a stamp, and it is always a higher one. This is the thing that is most disturbing to all of us. I fear that it will turn the people of Canada still more against this department. We would like some assurance from the minister that things will be done. I think if he would stand up and say that the five-day week was a mistake and that he will see it is corrected, that would do something in itself to get across to the people of Canada that there would be some improvements. I wait and hope that he will take this opportunity.
I hope that we will get a little more efficiency and a little less tendency to reach for a bigger stamp cost. I hope we will have no more regrettable performances such as that which we are reminded of every day when we see the Lapalme workers parading around the Parliament grounds. History says, perhaps somewhat mythically, that a certain queen of France lost her head for telling the people of that country to eat cake. What the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) advised these poor workers to eat is far less appetising than that, and this is hardly the view of an enlightened employer toward people who have grave difficulties in working for the people of Canada.
So I look upon this legislation with feelings of regret. I wish that this minister could have produced something more than yet another appeal to the people of Canada to pay more for their postage stamps. There are so few governmental services which are given to the people of Canada at low cost that it is too bad the art, the capacity of communicating one with another should be taxed ever more heavily. Therefore I do not welcome this piece of legislation, nor do I commend the minister for his actions in bringing it forward.

Mr. Speaker, I believe there is a disposition to reach the point tonight at which a vote on the amendment could be ordered. My remarks will not interfere with our reaching that point. However, I should like to add to the comments that have already been made by my colleagues, the hon. member for Battleford-Kindersley (Mr. Thomson) and the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Harding), by saying very clearly that we shall support the amendment for a six months' hoist and that when the vote on the second reading of the bill com.es, if it does come, we shall vote against the bill itself.
As has been pointed out several times today, it is only a few years ago that people could mail first-class letters in the city for four cents and anywhere in Canada for five cents. By next July, if this bill goes through, that four cents will be doubled to eight cents and the five cents rate will become eight cents. That is an increase that I think deserves the word "unconscionable" when one considers what even a few cents mean to many of our people, particularly those whose pensions were increased last December by only 42 cents a month.
This is not a justifiable increase, and we shall oppose it. However, Sir, there are a couple of other things I would like to say. The hon. member for Hillsborough (Mr. Macquarrie) referred feelingly to the remarks that were given some publicity today, remarks made by representatives of the Canadian Union of Postal Workers. As I recall it, the representatives of that union said-and they said it on the background of the experience they have had-that it is not their business to improve the image of the Post Office; that it is their job to get the

May 31, 1971

best possible deal for their members who work for the Post Office.
One cannot quarrel with that position taken by the unions, but I think it ought to be a challenge to the soon-to-be Postmaster General. He belongs to a government which has mouthed the phrase "participatory democracy." I suggest that those words from the union are a challenge to him to establish the kind of relationship with the workers in the Post Office so that they will feel not only that they must secure better wages and working conditions for themselves but that they will want to help improve the image of the department as a whole. You cannot expect them to do that unless they are presented with an opportunity or a challenge. I suggest that the ball is in the court of the soon-to-be Postmaster General.

speechtext:
I should like to comment briefly on the changes proposed by this bill with respect to mailing services which presently are free. I notice that a number of changes are being made. There is one particular complaint which I have received many times in recent weeks. A number of correspondents have asked why they must pay postage when mailing their income tax form but not on the census form. The official answer is that the taxation data centre in Ottawa to which income tax returns are sent has been designated as a field office, not the head office of the Post Office Department, and therefore a postage stamp is required. Apparently, because the census return involves statistics it is possible to send it to field offices all over the country without postage.
It looks as though there is another explanation behind this, Mr. Speaker. Citizens know that if they do not file an income tax return they will be in trouble, and so the government charges what the traffic will bear. There is not the same element of compulsion with regard to the census return. I know there is a penalty for non-return, but people do not seem to fear it and in order to induce them to send the return to Toronto, Winnipeg, Calgary or any other centre there is no charge for mailing.
The reasoning behind such decisions is not commendable. If census returns can be mailed postage free, I suggest that the same should apply to income tax returns. Although we are speaking of only a few cents it is another form of regressive taxation. For the wealthier people, the millionaires, another 6 or 8 cents for postage on an income tax return does not mean anything, but to the old age pensioner on the guaranteed income supplement the fact of having to pay postage on a tax return is adding insult to injury. The bill makes it possible to have some reconsideration of the question of what can or cannot be free. I hope common sense will prevail when the bill gets to the standing committee-that is, provided it gets there.
The essential feature of the bill is to increase the postage on the first ounce of first-class mail to seven
Canada-Finland Income Tax Act, 1971
cents on July 1, and to eight cents on January 1 next. This party is against this being done, so we shall vote for the six months' hoist, and if we get to second reading of the bill we shall vote against it.

maintopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-EAST PAKISTAN CONFLICT-DISCUSSIONS WITH INDIAN AND PAKISTANI REPRESENTATIVES-PROVISION OF RELIEF SUPPLIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on May 4 I asked the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp) about Canada's role in providing relief supplies for the victims of the cruel war in East Pakistan. Regrettably, Sir, the question still has painful relevance today. News items from the India-East Pakistan border tell of terrible suffering on the part of vast numbers of people. A despatch from New Delhi today declares that over four million East Pakistanis have fled from East Pakistan since martial law was imposed. The Indian Labour and Rehabilitation Minister, R. K. Khadilkar, is quoted as saying "What the eventual figure will be is
anybody's guess. It may be five or even eight million." Reports of cholera epidemic add tragedy to an already deplorable story of mass human suffering. Crowded living conditions have fostered other diseases.
The minister already quoted accused Pakistani troops of pursuing the refugees across the frontier into India. Alluding to the possibility of India taking defensive or preventive measures, he said, "Nobody wants war but if they start hot pursuit, as they are now doing, in such a situation can one keep absolutely mum and just protect?" Thus the prospects of international military action are very much and very dangerously present. So, along with a gripping story of fearful human suffering we have here a grave threat to world peace.
As I said in the House on Friday, I welcome the government announcement regarding the $2 million contribution to relief funds. Certainly the whole burden must not be borne by India. It is a matter of international concern and should also be one for international action. So far I have not noted any Commonwealth interest or initiative. I wonder what, if anything, Canada has been doing to have this matter discussed in a Commonwealth context.
The initiative of Secretary General U Thant is welcome. The visit of the three-member team from the office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees was also a proper step. But the need for international inspection on both sides of the border is compellingly urgent. I think none of us here enjoy seeing Pakistan become the object of widespread and sharp criticism from the thoughtful and sensitive in the international community.
There is obviously a very serious situation in Pakistan, and while that country may well assert that the political aspects are not the subject of international scrutiny or concern, the humanitarian aspect is one which should prompt the government of Pakistan to welcome the good intentions and efforts of people from many parts of the world.
I hope that Canada will not rest its case with the $2 million contribution or desist from its efforts to broaden the base of aid and enlarge the scope of the assistance which so many people across the world desire to extend to the victims of this grim, human tragedy. I hope that we will continue our aid program through the approved channels. We should also use our good offices with Pakistan, a fellow Commonwealth state, to open the doors and remove all grounds for criticism that political considerations are standing in the way of maximizing aid to an unhappy people.
Mr. Ray Perrauli (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister
of Labour): Mr. Speaker, since May 4, when the hon. member for Hillsborough (Mr. Macquarrie) asked for more elaboration on the situation in East Pakistan and particularly whether the authorities there would accept relief supplies, it can be said that some progress has been made toward providing relief assistance for the victims of the Pakistani conflict. As you are aware, it was announced on May 28 that the government is providing $2 million to help meet the immediate needs of the refugees crossing into neighbouring states of India from

May 31, 1971

East Pakistan. Included in the Canadian contribution will be foodstuffs, medicines, medical supplies and a cash donation. This is, of course, additional to the earlier contribution of $50,000 to the Canadian Red Cross, supplementing its gift of $10,000 to the Indian Red Cross for relief to refugees.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp) had earlier indicated that the government of Pakistan was reluctant to accept relief assistance or to permit relief administrators into East Pakistan, considering that their own resources were adequate to meet immediate needs. This situation has now changed and the government of Pakistan has recently indicated that assistance from abroad would be welcome.
Our High Commissioner in Islamabad has been in contact with officials of the Pakistani government who have indicated that external assistance will be required in two categories: (1), humanitarian relief and (2), reconstruction and rehabilitation. The government of Pakistan has appealed to the United Nations and to the world food program for assistance in the first category. With regard to reconstruction and rehabilitation of East Pakistan, the Pakistan government has prepared a list of priority items which is now receiving scrutiny of the appropriate governmental authorities.
The Secretary General of the United Nations has appointed a co-ordinator of United Nations relief activity and it is expected that he will visit East Pakistan in the very near future. Canada has already indicated that any assistance which the Canadian government may give will be closely co-ordinated with that provided through the United Nations.
Assurances have been received from the government of Pakistan that any assistance given will be used only for rehab.litation and relief, and the co-ordination arrangements to which they have agreed would appear to be adequate to ensure proper distribution for the purposes intended.

maintopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-EAST PAKISTAN CONFLICT-DISCUSSIONS WITH INDIAN AND PAKISTANI REPRESENTATIVES-PROVISION OF RELIEF SUPPLIES
subtopic: AIRPORTS-TORONTO INTERNATIONAL-METHOD OF LETTING CONTRACTS FOR SKYCAP SERVICES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on May 18 I directed a question to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Jamieson) which hon. members will find reported in
Hansard in the following terms:
I have a question for the Minister of Transport. In view of the report that a United States firm has displaced a Canadian-owned company at the international airport at Toronto, involving the majority of airport skycaps, would the minister indicate the method by which such contracts are let?
Mr. Speaker indicated he doubted whether the question was in order and suggested it might be considered at the time of adjournment. I agree with him 100 per cent.
First, I should like to say we are extremely pleased to learn that in this corner of the House there is to be one more member, from the constituency of Brant. He was elected with a majority of about 5,000 and he will probably be in a position to speak forcefully for the people in that area when he enters the House very shortly.
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
With regard to the question I asked, it appears that Consolidated Fueling Services of New York took over the skycap contracts at the International airport in Toronto for all but two airlines. They are Air Canada and Canadian Pacific Airlines. At that time Consolidated Fueling Services agreed verbally that they would hire the people who had been laid off by Airline Services, who previously held the contract, thus enabling men who had spent years of service at the airport to retain employment.
However, this was not the result of the takeover which is really effective as a result of agreements between the airlines involved and the people employed as skycaps. It would seem that the situation involved in this so-called contract at Toronto airport is similar to that which arose in Montreal not long ago. The men concerned in that affair, the Lapalme drivers, are still marching in front of the House of Commons day in and day out. Someone else took over the contract to provide the services which they were providing and the displaced workers are still expressing their concern.
The same thing could happen in Toronto unless the Department of Transport undertakes to do something about the type of contract they let at so-called public expense airports. For the department to wash its hands of the whole affair is not in the Canadian interest. We are well aware that in Toronto, Consolidated Fuelling Services of New York, a strictly U.S.-owned firm, did not employ the people that they had undertaken to employ and as a result the airline services which did employ labour for Air Canada and CP Air had to lay off, according to my information, some eight people at the terminal.
I am asking whether or not the government, although the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Duquet), would indicate to the House this evening why a United States firm has been allowed completely to take over services at the International Airport at Toronto that were not put out to tender; why it has allowed independent airlines operating into Canada to employ skycaps without tender; why it has allowed air services which would hire skycaps to employ people off the street rather than engage labour that was fully qualified; and why the Department of Transport claims it is interested in providing services to the people when there are two groups of skycaps at Toronto International Airport meeting cabs that arrive at the airport and asking the passenger whether they are travelling by Air Canada or CP Air, thus causing a nuisance to the travelling public.
The people of Canada are entitled to know whether or not the employment of skycap services in this country is going to be commensurate with the demand. They are entitled to know whether these services are sufficient to serve the travelling public. Although the people who were picked off the street may well have been Canadians, in my humble opinion this is another case of union-busting. Consolidated Fuelling Services of New York do not hire union labour or have certification with any labour union in Canada. To say the least, it is a disgrace that

May 31, 1971
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion while we have airline services in Canada today which hire labour from the Canadian Brotherhood of Railways, Transport and General Workers Union, the company to which I have referred, unhindered by the Department of Transport, is allowed to hire people off the street who are unqualified or inexperienced, which in turn results in the lay-off of long-term employees who themselves have to walk the street.

maintopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-EAST PAKISTAN CONFLICT-DISCUSSIONS WITH INDIAN AND PAKISTANI REPRESENTATIVES-PROVISION OF RELIEF SUPPLIES
subtopic: AIRPORTS-TORONTO INTERNATIONAL-METHOD OF LETTING CONTRACTS FOR SKYCAP SERVICES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member from Moose Jaw (Mr. Skoberg) raised this question on May 18. Since that date I have had an opportunity to make inquiries with officials in the Department of Transport who are familiar with the detailed operation of the International Airport at Toronto. I am informed that the skycap service is handled directly by the airlines and not by the department. The reason for this is that it is felt that the service is one that can be directly attributed to the passenger and that the airlines are in a better position to provide this service.
The hon. member is aware that up to a short time ago the skycap service for the majority of the airlines at Toronto was provided by Air Terminal Transport Limited. Recently the contract expired, and although Air Canada extended the contract the other airlines preferred to solicit bids from other companies in this type of business, including Air Terminal Transport. As a result of the bids a contract was awarded to Consolidated Aviation and Services, the Canadian subsidiary of Allied Aviation Services.
The hon. member has made a number of observations which I have noted. I will, of course, bring these to the attention of the departmental officials who are directly concerned with this subject, and if there are additional points which have not been mentioned this evening I would be pleased to receive them.

maintopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-EAST PAKISTAN CONFLICT-DISCUSSIONS WITH INDIAN AND PAKISTANI REPRESENTATIVES-PROVISION OF RELIEF SUPPLIES
subtopic: POST OFFICE-LAST DAILY PICK-UP OF MAIL IN CITIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, once upon a time at this hour the House used to ring with welcome over the great exchanges between the hon. member for Hillsborough (Mr. Macquarrie) and the former Minister of Communications and Postmaster General, the hon. member for Duvernay (Mr. Kierans). So great was the excitement produced by these exchanges that the National Centre for the Performing Arts had to time its evening breaks and its performances in order that people could rush up here for 10 or 15 minutes to hear what went on. We all know what happened to the former Minister of Communications and Postmaster General.
In inviting our friend, the soon-to-become Postmaster General, here this evening I promised him I would not, and do not want to, perform in the role of the hon. member for Hillsborough. I should like to clear up one question in my mind. Broadly stated the question is, does the government serve the people or do the people exist to serve the government? More specifically, did the government or his department really have to change the timing of afternoon mail collection from some time after five
o'clock to around three o'clock in our great Canadian
cities?
The minister, his department and his staff in various parts of Canada have received correspondence in respect of this early mail collection. I should like to quote from two letters. The first is from a Mr. Paul D. Silver, president of Silver's Agencies Limited of Halifax. He states in part:
For some unexplained, and in my opinion completely unfounded, reason business "boxes" are only cleared once daily (Monday to Friday) and that at 3 p.m. or two hours prior to the close of normal office business.
Delivery to Montreal/Toronto, on 5 p.m. mailing, would therefore require 38 hours as against the previous 18 hours.
Local deliveries, within the city, also come on a 38-hour delivery basis.
Is it anticipated that, for a whim of Ottawa, every company should reorganize to mail before the 3 p.m. deadline or should we all direct our staff to the post office, after 5 p.m., causing traffic tie-ups, diverting people from their normal home routing and adding to their expenses?
The other quotation is from a letter written by Mr. Byron D. Anthony, director, labour-management bureau at the Dalhousie institute of public affairs, Dalhousie University. It was written to the postmaster in Halifax and in part states:
To be more specific, mail posted in a city mail box at 5.20 p.m. Friday, May 14th addressed to 15 separate addresses, at noon today, Wednesday, May 19th had been delivered to only four recipients.
That gives an idea of the magnitude of this problem and the fact that people still have their normal office routines to follow. Having regard to the question I posed last week, the soon-to-become Postmaster General was really telling us that the mailing habits of Canadians should be changed. Perhaps the habits of the new Postmaster General and his department should be changed back to what used to be the case. I ask the Postmaster General to assess this new time in light of experience, and should the resistance of the public be greater than its acceptance to the new hours will a change be made back to former hours?

maintopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-EAST PAKISTAN CONFLICT-DISCUSSIONS WITH INDIAN AND PAKISTANI REPRESENTATIVES-PROVISION OF RELIEF SUPPLIES
subtopic: POST OFFICE-LAST DAILY PICK-UP OF MAIL IN CITIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have already partially answered that question as it was asked by the hon. member the other day in the House. I can add to that answer that the frequency of clearances of street letter boxes varies at each assured mail centre, but generally boxes located in residential areas are cleared once daily in the morning and striped boxes located on main thoroughfares and in business areas are cleared at least twice daily, in the morning and in the early afternoon, Monday to Friday, and once in the morning on Saturdays, Sundays and holidays. Times shown on both types of boxes reflect final clearance deadlines for assured next delivery day service to designated centres.
A final early evening clearance is made from striped boxes only at most assured mail centres, Monday to Friday. This mail is processed in the normal way, and

May 31, 1971

although we are able to give a good portion of it following-day delivery in certain areas it is not guaranteed next delivery day service.
The need for a later pick-up of mail after assured mail collection deadlines will be determined on the individual merits of each area where the assured mail program is implemented. That is why we are still having difficulty with the program. As I say, we might have had better box clearance in some areas. All we were doing in many instances was merely accumulating a large volume of mail in the post offices during the night which meant that
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion more employees had to work on the night shift without providing better service.
So we hope after a period of adjustment to have a more assured mail program. If the people of Canada will bear with us a little longer, I believe I can assure hon. members and the public that in a short time, a month or two, things will be stabilized to a large degree and the service will be very much better than it is at present.
Motion agreed to and the House adjourned at 10.25 p.m.
